newsitem.title: CHINA: HK property prices to rise in next 3 yrs - Salomon.
newsitem.headline: HK property prices to rise in next 3 yrs - Salomon.

text.p: Salomon Brothers said it expects property prices to continue rising over the next three years, with government plans to increase land supply unlikely to hurt prices due to a housing backlog.

"We do not believe an increase in land supply will be detrimental to prices because of the huge housing backlog. Moreover, the initiative is likely to slow down price increases, and should not have a downward effect," analyst Michael Green said in a report.

He said housing demand should remain high over the next three years and forecast a rise of 10-12 percent in residential prices in 1997, followed by a 15-17 percent increase in 1998 and a 15-20 percent in increase in 1999.

Green said the response to recent property sales had been high since the government announced a five-year land sales programme last month which would boost residential land supply by 140 percent compared with the previous five years.
"This is an indication that buyers are under no illusions about the lack of supply in the next three to four years."

But Salomon said it was recommending a neutral position on property developer stocks compared with a prior buy rating due to expected price volatility ahead of the release of more details on the government's housing policy due in October, high share prices and a mild increase in U.S. interest rates.
However, Hong Kong's housing plans could enhance profitability in the long term, Green said.

"Even in the absence of a backlog as large as Hong Kong currently has on its hands, it does not necessarily follow that an increase in housing supply would be detrimental to developers' profitability," he said.
Higher volume often results in only slightly lower profit margins and developers could reposition their existing landbank and target the upper-end of the market, Salomon said.
"They can widen their margins by focusing on this end of the market as the economy is stimulated and economic growth continues to add to the wealth of individuals."
